title: Verilog HDL
description: Learn to describe digital hardware in Verilog: modules, data types, operators, assign, always blocks, testbenches and finite state machines, with runnable examples you can simulate in HDL Studio.

questions.prompt: Which keyword closes a Verilog module?
questions.explanation: Every module ends with endmodule.

questions.prompt: In module m(input a, output y); what is y?
questions.explanation: y is declared with the output direction.

questions.prompt: What is a top module?
choices: A module that no other module instantiates
The first module in the file
questions.explanation: Top modules are not instantiated by anything; in simulation this is normally the testbench.

questions.prompt: Why are named port connections like .a(x) preferred?
choices: They are required by the language
They do not depend on port order
questions.explanation: Named connections cannot be mixed up if the port order changes.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates an 8-bit signal?
questions.explanation: [7:0] means bits 7 down to 0, so 8 bits.

questions.prompt: Where can a reg be assigned?
questions.explanation: Procedural assignment targets regs.

questions.prompt: What value does an unassigned reg have at time 0?
questions.explanation: Uninitialised signals start as unknown (x).
Concatenation puts a first (most significant) then b.

questions.prompt: What does the keyword integer declare?
questions.explanation: integer is a 32-bit signed variable, often a loop counter.
Bitwise AND is 1 only where both bits are 1.

questions.prompt: What does a && b give when a=4'b1010 and b=4'b0101?
questions.explanation: Both are non-zero, so the logical AND is true (1).

questions.prompt: What does |4'b0000 give?
questions.explanation: OR-reduction is 1 only if some bit is 1.

questions.prompt: What does sel ? a : b select when sel is 0?
questions.explanation: The conditional operator returns the second option when the condition is false.

questions.prompt: Which comparison treats x as different from 0 and 1 exactly?
questions.explanation: === compares all four states exactly; == can return x.

questions.prompt: What can the left side of assign be?
questions.explanation: assign drives nets (wires).

questions.prompt: In and g1(y, a, b); which terminal is the output?
questions.explanation: The first terminal of a gate primitive is the output.

questions.prompt: When is the expression in an assign evaluated?
choices: Whenever a signal on its right side changes
questions.explanation: Continuous assignments re-evaluate on any input change.

questions.prompt: Which is dataflow style?
questions.explanation: assign with expressions is dataflow; gate primitives are structural.

questions.prompt: Why is driving the same wire from two assigns a problem?
questions.explanation: Multiple drivers on one bit can fight and produce unknown values.

questions.prompt: Which sensitivity list makes combinational logic?
questions.explanation: @(*) re-runs the block when any input changes.

questions.prompt: What triggers always @(posedge clk)?
questions.explanation: posedge means the 0-to-1 transition.

questions.prompt: What causes an accidental latch?
choices: An output not assigned on every path
questions.explanation: If a path leaves an output unassigned, the old value must be remembered.

questions.prompt: Which assignment style belongs in clocked blocks?
questions.explanation: Non-blocking assignments model flip-flops that update together.

questions.prompt: After a <= b; b <= a; with a=0 and b=1, what are a and b?
questions.explanation: Both right sides use old values, so the two swap.

questions.prompt: Which is true of blocking assignment (=)?
choices: The update waits for the end of the time step
It cannot be used in always blocks
questions.explanation: Blocking assignments take effect immediately, so later statements see the new value.

questions.prompt: In a 4-bit shift register q <= {q[2:0], din}, how far does each bit move per clock?
questions.explanation: All right sides use the old q, so every bit shifts by exactly one place.

questions.prompt: What does $finish do?
questions.explanation: $finish stops the simulation.

questions.prompt: Which block normally generates stimulus once?
questions.explanation: initial runs once from time 0.

questions.prompt: What does always #5 clk = ~clk; do?
questions.explanation: The always block repeats forever, giving a clock with period 10.

questions.prompt: Why wait #1 before checking an output after changing inputs?
choices: To avoid x values at reset
questions.explanation: Delays let the design react before the test samples.

questions.prompt: Why check with !== rather than != ?
choices: x outputs then fail the check
questions.explanation: !== treats x as different, so unknown outputs are caught.

questions.prompt: What does the state register hold?
questions.explanation: A clocked block stores the current state.

questions.prompt: In a Moore machine outputs depend on...
questions.explanation: Moore outputs come from the state alone.

questions.prompt: Why include a default branch in the next-state case?
questions.explanation: A default returns the machine to a known state.

questions.prompt: In the 101 detector, which state means the last two bits were 1,0?
questions.explanation: S0 saw nothing useful, S1 saw 1, S2 saw 1 then 0.

questions.prompt: Why does S2 go to S1 on x=1 in the overlapping detector?
choices: The new 1 may start another pattern
questions.explanation: The final 1 of 101 can also be the first 1 of the next 101.

lessons.title: Modules, Ports and Structure
objectives: Write a module with ANSI-style ports
Instantiate one module inside another using named port connections
Explain what a top module is
lessons.body:
A Verilog design is built from modules. A module has a name, a port list that says which signals enter and leave, and a body that describes what the hardware does. Everything between the keywords module and endmodule belongs to it.

Ports have a direction: input, output or inout. In the modern ANSI style the direction and type are written directly in the port list, for example module and_gate(input a, input b, output y). Inside the body you describe behaviour, for example with an assign statement.

Modules are reused by instantiating them inside other modules. An instance needs the module name, an instance name and the port connections. Named connections such as .a(x) are safer than positional ones because the order cannot be mixed up. A module that nobody instantiates is a top module; in simulation that is normally the testbench.

definitions.meaning: The basic building block of a Verilog design, from module to endmodule.
A named connection point of a module with a direction: input, output or inout.
One use of a module inside another module, with its own name and connections.
A module that is not instantiated by any other module.

lessons.exampleNote: u1 is an instance of and_gate. Each .port(signal) pair connects a port of the module to a signal in the parent.
mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after the port list: write module name(...); with the semicolon.
Connecting ports by position and swapping two signals: prefer named connections like .a(x).
Declaring an output as wire and then assigning it in an always block: use output reg for that.

practice.a: endmodule closes the module started by module.
They do not depend on port order, so reordering ports cannot silently break the design.

exercises: In HDL Studio open the demo, press Run and read the truth table.
Change the gate to OR by editing one operator and run again.
summary: A module has ports and a body.
Instances reuse modules; named connections are safer.
A module nobody instantiates is a top module.

lessons.title: wire, reg and Vectors
objectives: Predict what x means in a simulation
lessons.body:
Verilog has two main kinds of signal. A wire is a connection: it is driven by an assign statement or by a module output and cannot be assigned inside an always block. A reg holds a value between assignments and is what you assign in always and initial blocks. Despite the name, a reg does not always become a hardware register; a combinational always block also assigns regs.

Signals can be vectors. reg [7:0] data declares an 8-bit signal whose bits are data[7] down to data[0]. You can select one bit, data[3], or a slice, data[7:4], and join signals with braces: {a, b}.

Simulation uses four values per bit: 0, 1, x for unknown and z for high impedance. Anything that has not been assigned yet starts as x. This simulator treats z as x. An integer is a 32-bit signed variable, handy for loop counters.

definitions.meaning: A net that is continuously driven; assigned with assign or by an instance output.
A variable assigned inside always or initial blocks; keeps its value.
A multi-bit signal such as [7:0].
The unknown logic value, for example before a signal has been assigned.

lessons.exampleNote: The first line prints the upper and lower nibbles; the second swaps them with a concatenation and prints 5a.
mistakes: Assigning a wire inside an always block: declare it reg, or use assign.
Writing reg [0:7] and reading bits backwards: put the MSB first, [7:0].
Expecting an uninitialised reg to be 0: it starts as x.

practice.q: What is the width of reg [3:0] a?
What does a reg hold before it is first assigned?

exercises: Run the demo and confirm the swapped nibbles.
Print a[0] and a[3] of a 4-bit value you choose.
summary: wire = driven connection, reg = assigned variable.
[msb:lsb] declares a vector; braces concatenate.
Unassigned signals are x.

lessons.title: Operators and Expressions
lessons.body:
Bitwise operators work on every bit position: & | ^ ~. Logical operators && || ! treat a whole value as true or false and give a single bit. For a = 4'b1010 and b = 4'b0101, a & b is 0000 but a && b is 1, because both values are non-zero.

Reduction operators collapse a vector into one bit. &a is 1 only if all bits are 1, |a is 1 if any bit is 1 and ^a gives the parity.

Other operators: + - * / % for arithmetic, << and >> for shifts, == != for equality and the conditional operator sel ? x : y, which is how a 2-to-1 multiplexer is written in one line. In this simulator all arithmetic is unsigned. If an operand contains x, an arithmetic or comparison result is x; === compares x exactly.

definitions.meaning: Acts on each bit pair of its operands.
Applies an operator across all bits of one vector to give one bit.
cond ? a : b selects a when cond is true, otherwise b.
{n{x}} repeats x n times.

lessons.exampleNote: Prints 0000 1, then 0 1 0, then 1010. The last line is a maximum selector.
mistakes: Using & where && is meant (or the reverse): & is per bit, && is true/false.
Forgetting that a + b in a 4-bit target loses the carry: widen the target or use a concatenation.
Comparing with == when x is possible: use === in testbenches.

practice.a: 1111, each bit is the OR of the pair.

exercises: Run the demo and explain each printed line.
Write a one-line assign that outputs the larger of two 4-bit inputs.
summary: Bitwise is per bit; logical gives one bit.
Reduction operators fold a vector into one bit.
Conditional operator is a compact multiplexer.

lessons.title: assign Statements and Gate Primitives
lessons.body:
A continuous assignment, written assign y = expression;, makes a wire follow an expression for as long as the simulation runs. Whenever any signal on the right-hand side changes, the expression is evaluated again and y is updated. That is exactly how a combinational circuit behaves, so assign is the simplest way to describe one.

Verilog also provides gate primitives such as and, or, not and xor. The first terminal is the output and the rest are inputs, for example and g1(y, a, b);. Writing gates by hand is called structural modelling; writing expressions with assign is dataflow modelling. Both describe the same hardware.

The left side of an assign must be a wire. Assigning a reg with assign is an error in this simulator and in real tools.

definitions.meaning: An assign statement that keeps a wire equal to an expression.
A built-in logic gate such as and, or, not, xor.
Describing logic with expressions and assign.
Describing a circuit as connected gates or modules.

lessons.exampleNote: The two forms are equivalent. A change on a or b immediately updates s and c.
lessons.diagram:
a ----+--[XOR]--> s
   b ----|--[AND]--> c
         |
  (either description gives this)
mistakes: Using assign to drive a reg: declare the target as wire.
Driving the same wire from two assign statements: only one driver per bit.
Believing assign executes once: it re-evaluates on every input change.

practice.q: Which terminal of a gate primitive is the output?

exercises: Run the demo to see sum and carry for all inputs.
Build NAND from an and gate followed by a not gate.
summary: assign keeps a wire equal to an expression.
Gate primitives list the output first.
Dataflow and structural styles give the same hardware.

lessons.title: always Blocks: Combinational and Sequential
objectives: Write a clocked register with posedge clk
lessons.body:
An always block runs repeatedly: every time something in its sensitivity list changes, the statements inside execute. For combinational logic use always @(*), which lists every signal the block reads automatically. Every output must get a value on every path through the block, otherwise the hardware must remember the old value and a latch appears.

For sequential logic write always @(posedge clk). The block only runs on the rising clock edge, so what you assign becomes flip-flop state. A synchronous reset is checked inside that block; an asynchronous reset is added to the list: always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n).

Signals assigned inside an always block must be declared reg. In this simulator an always @(*) block also runs once at time 0 so combinational outputs start with real values.

definitions.meaning: The events that make an always block run, for example posedge clk.
An always block whose outputs depend only on current inputs.
An always block triggered by a clock edge that creates flip-flops.
Unintended memory created when an output is not assigned on every path.

lessons.exampleNote: The first block is a 2-to-1 mux; the second is a D flip-flop with a synchronous reset.
lessons.diagram:
clk  _|-|_|-|_|-|_
  d    ---X----X--------
  q    ----X----X-------
  (q copies d at each rising edge)
mistakes: Leaving out an else branch in combinational logic: you create a latch, assign a default first.
Using always @(a) when the block also reads b: use @(*).
Mixing clocked and combinational styles in one block.

practice.q: Why must an output be assigned on every path in combinational logic?
practice.a: Otherwise the circuit has to remember the old value, which is a latch.

exercises: Run the demo and watch q follow d after each clock.
Remove the else branch from the mux and think about what hardware that implies.
summary: always @(*) is combinational, always @(posedge clk) is sequential.
Assign every output on every path to avoid latches.
Variables assigned in always blocks are reg.

lessons.title: Blocking (=) vs Non-Blocking (<=)
objectives: Choose the right one for sequential and combinational logic
Predict a swap and a shift register
lessons.body:
A blocking assignment (=) updates the left side immediately, so the next statement already sees the new value. A non-blocking assignment (<=) first evaluates the right side, then updates the left side at the end of the time step, after every always block has had a chance to read the old values.

That is exactly how flip-flops behave: all of them sample their inputs on the same clock edge. So the rule is simple. Use <= in clocked always blocks and = in combinational always blocks. Do not mix both styles for the same signal.

Two classic examples show the difference. With a <= b; b <= a; the two values swap. With a = b; b = a; both end up holding the old b. In a shift register q <= {q[2:0], din}, every bit moves one place per clock because all right sides use the old q.

definitions.meaning: = : executes in order and updates immediately.
<= : right side is sampled now, the update happens at the end of the time step.
Result depends on the order in which simultaneous events happen to run.
Registers chained so each takes the previous one's value on every clock.

lessons.example:
always @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b;
  b <= a;      // swap
end
lessons.exampleNote: Because both right sides are read before either update, a and b exchange values on each clock edge.
lessons.diagram:
clk edge:
   a_old=0 b_old=1
   a <= b  ->  a_new = 1
   b <= a  ->  b_new = 0
   (old values are used)
mistakes: Using = in clocked blocks: use <= so flip-flops update together.
Using <= for combinational outputs and reading them in the same block: use =.
Assigning the same reg from two different always blocks.

practice.q: Which assignment do you use inside always @(posedge clk)?
After a <= b; b <= a; with a=0, b=1, what are a and b?

exercises: Run the swap demo, then change <= to = and explain the new result.
Draw a 4-bit shift register and mark which value each flip-flop samples.
summary: = is immediate; <= updates at the end of the time step.
Use <= for clocked logic, = for combinational.
Non-blocking models simultaneous flip-flops.

lessons.title: Writing Testbenches
lessons.body:
A testbench is a module without ports that instantiates the design under test (DUT), drives its inputs and checks its outputs. It is never synthesised; it only runs in simulation, so it may use delays and system tasks.

Stimulus is written in initial blocks, which run once from time 0. #5 waits 5 time units. A clock is usually made with always #5 clk = ~clk; after setting clk = 0 in an initial block. The task $display prints a line, $monitor prints whenever one of its arguments changes and $finish ends the simulation.

A good testbench checks results itself: compare the output with the expected value using !== (which also catches x), count errors and print PASS or FAIL at the end. Then you never need to read waveforms to know that a change broke something.

definitions.meaning: Design under test, the module the testbench exercises.
The input values a testbench applies over time.
One that compares outputs with expected values and reports PASS or FAIL.
System task that ends the simulation.

lessons.exampleNote: The clock toggles every 5 units; reset is released at 12; after waiting the testbench checks the counter.
lessons.diagram:
time  0   5   10  15  20
  clk   0   1   0   1   0
  rst   1   1   1   0   0
        (reset released at t=12)
mistakes: Forgetting $finish when a clock runs forever: the simulation stops only at the safety limit.
Using != instead of !== so an x output looks like a pass: use !==.
Checking outputs at the same instant inputs change: wait #1 first.

practice.a: Toggles clk every 5 time units, forever.
It treats x as different from 0 or 1, so unknown outputs fail.

exercises: Run the demo and read the log.
Add one more test vector that should fail and see FAIL printed.
summary: A testbench instantiates the DUT and drives inputs.
initial for stimulus, always for clocks.
Self-checking tests print PASS or FAIL.

lessons.title: Coding Finite State Machines
objectives: Structure an FSM as state register, next-state logic and output logic
lessons.body:
A finite state machine is usually written as three parts. A state register, a clocked always block, stores the current state. Next-state logic, a combinational always block with a case statement, decides the next state from the current state and the inputs. Output logic produces the outputs, either from the state alone (Moore) or from the state and the inputs (Mealy).

Give states readable names with parameter, for example S0, S1, S2, and always include a default branch that returns to a safe state. Keep reset in the state register so the machine starts in a known state.

The demo is a Mealy detector for the bit pattern 1-0-1 with overlap: it moves S0 to S1 on a 1, S1 to S2 on a 0 and raises its output when it is in S2 and sees another 1.

definitions.meaning: Flip-flops that hold the current state.
Outputs depend only on the current state.
Outputs depend on the current state and the inputs.
The end of one match can be the start of the next.

lessons.exampleNote: S2 means the last two bits were 1,0. A 1 in S2 completes 101 and also counts as the first 1 of the next pattern, so the next state is S1.
mistakes: Missing default branch: add one that returns to the reset state.
Putting outputs in the clocked block by accident, adding an extra cycle of delay.
Using many unrelated assigns instead of one case statement.

practice.q: Which part decides the next state?
Is y here a Moore or Mealy output?
practice.a: Mealy, because it depends on the input x as well as the state.

exercises: Run the demo and find the positions where 101 is detected.
Change the pattern to 110 and update the states.
summary: FSM = state register + next-state logic + output logic.
Name states with parameters; always have a default.
Moore outputs use state only; Mealy also uses inputs.
